newsitem.title: USA: Korea talks adjourn after faltering on agenda.
newsitem.headline: Korea talks adjourn after faltering on agenda.

text.p: The four main combatants in the 1950-53 Korean War have failed to agree on an agenda for formal peace negotiations but will continue preparatory talks next month, officials said on Thursday.

They said diplomats from the United States, China, North Korea and South Korea would meet again during the week of Sept. 15 in New York to complete work on the logistics for negotiations aimed at replacing the fraying Korean War armistice with a more durable peace on the bitterly divided Korean peninsula.

"We found that there were some significant differences over whether the agenda should be of a general nature or more specific," a senior U.S. official said at the end of three days of talks at New York's Columbia University. He declined to give further details.

The U.S. official and the head of the Chinese delegation, assistant foreign minister Chen Jian, said the four countries had agreed on starting formal peace talks in Geneva four to six weeks after the end of next month's meeting.

The discussions that began on Tuesday were limited to setting a date, time, place and agenda for full discussions on replacing the armistice. China was communist North Korea's ally in the Korean War and the United States supported the capitalist South.

Washington and Seoul worked for more than a year to bring the isolationist North Korean government to the negotiating table. U.S. officials have said it was "entirely possible" that famine-stricken North Korea was joining the talks to procure more food aid.

The senior U.S. official told reporters that food aid was raised by the Pyongyang delegation in informal meetings on Thursday morning, but not in the preparatory talks themselves. U.N. agencies said on Monday that a drought in North Korea had devasted 70 percent of the country's maize crop.
The agencies said even heavy rainfall would not be enough to alleviate the drought. Some reports have likened the disaster to the famine in Ethiopia in the 1980s.
This week's meetings marked an important phase in the peace process because it was the first time representatives of China had joined the talks.
"There are some disagreements over the agenda but we have agreed to meet again," Chen told reporters.

The senior U.S. official said that although there was some disappointment over failure to agree on the agenda, "there is some confidence that the four-party structure can work... and that we will finish the job in the next session."

Pyongyang and Seoul traded accusations before Thursday's session. North Korea blasted the United States and the South for planning joint military exercises later this month, and Seoul said Pyongyang's demands that American troops be withdrawn were preventing progress in the talks.
About 37,000 U.S. troops are stationed in South Korea to help defend the country. The demilitarized zone that divides North and South is one of the last vestiges of the Cold War.
In Washington, State Department spokesman James Rubin dismissed the criticism of the joint exercises.
"We do not regard actions we take with regard to South Korea as threatening," he said. "On the contrary, we have a defence alliance, not an offence alliance, with South Korea."

The U.S.-South Korean exercise is scheduled for Aug. 18 to 29 and involves 16,500 U.S. military personnel and tens of thousands of South Koreans. The joint drills have been conducted every year since 1976.
